modules.objective: Build the right mindset — helping patients decide, not convincing them to buy.
modules.shortDescription: Transition from transactional sales to trusted clinical advisor. Patient outcome always matters more than target.
concept: A counsellor operates at the intersection of five roles: Listener, Guide, Communicator, Trust Builder, Decision Facilitator.

The 70/30 Listening Law: The counsellor listens 70% of the consultation and speaks 30% with precise clinical insight.

questions.question: What is the counsellor's role according to the GLEUHR mindset?
questions.clinicalRationale: The counsellor listens first, consults second, and facilitates the patient's own decision.

questions.question: Why is empathy considered a sales skill here?
options: It replaces the need for product knowledge
It builds the trust that makes an honest recommendation land
It's only useful for difficult patients
questions.clinicalRationale: Empathy builds the trust that makes a genuine recommendation credible.

questions.question: A patient who doesn't book today should be treated as:
options: Someone still deciding, not a failure
A reason to escalate to a manager
questions.clinicalRationale: Patient-first selling respects the patient's own pace of decision-making.

questions.question: What should come before any recommendation?
questions.clinicalRationale: Recommendations follow understanding — never precede it.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the GLEUHR philosophy?
options: "We help the patient make a confident decision."
questions.clinicalRationale: This is the module's core message, restated directly.

questions.question: What carries more weight than the words themselves in a first impression?
questions.clinicalRationale: Delivery — tone and energy — shapes trust as much as, or more than, the words used.

questions.question: Which opening line reflects professional presence?
options: "Hi ma'am, welcome to GLEUHR — may I understand your concern a little more?"
"How can I help you today, quickly?"
questions.clinicalRationale: It's warm, specific, and invites the patient to share — professional and human.

questions.question: Why does the same reassuring line fail when delivered mechanically?
options: Delivery without warmth reads as indifference
questions.clinicalRationale: Words alone don't build trust — delivery does.

questions.question: Professional presence should be:
options: Adjusted based on how busy you are
questions.clinicalRationale: Consistency is what makes presence trustworthy rather than performative.

questions.question: In-clinic, which non-verbal signal builds the most immediate trust?
options: Calm eye contact and open posture
Standing behind the desk at all times
questions.clinicalRationale: Eye contact and open posture signal genuine attention.

questions.question: Under the 70/30 rule, who should be talking more?
questions.clinicalRationale: The patient talks roughly 70% of the time — the counsellor guides through questions.

questions.question: What is the correct question sequence?
questions.clinicalRationale: Open the topic, probe deeper, clarify specifics, then confirm understanding.

questions.question: Why avoid clinical jargon the patient hasn't used?
options: It makes you sound less qualified
It can confuse or intimidate rather than inform
It takes too long to say
questions.clinicalRationale: Jargon the patient doesn't share yet can create distance, not authority.

questions.question: "Mere hair bahut fall ho rahe hain" is best followed by:
options: "Aapko ye hair fall kab se noticeable lag raha hai?"
"Let me send you our price list."
questions.clinicalRationale: A discovery question keeps the conversation open rather than jumping to a pitch.

questions.question: Staying in "conversation control" means:
options: Guiding the flow without dominating it
questions.clinicalRationale: Control means guiding structure, not dominating airtime.

questions.question: What does the READ → RECOGNISE → RESPOND framework train?
options: Reading the emotional signal before responding
questions.clinicalRationale: It trains counsellors to read the emotion before crafting a response.

questions.question: "How much does it cost?" could hide all of these EXCEPT:
options: A definite yes regardless of price
questions.clinicalRationale: A definite yes regardless of price isn't a hidden concern — it's the absence of one.

questions.question: Which combination makes up a patient's full emotional context?
questions.clinicalRationale: These five elements sit beneath most patient statements.

questions.question: Responding only to the literal question risks:
questions.clinicalRationale: Literal-only responses can miss what's actually driving the hesitation.

questions.question: Best first move when price comes up early?

Offer a discount to defuse it
questions.clinicalRationale: A quick clarifying question uncovers the real concern before you respond to it.

questions.question: How many discovery pillars make up the GLEUHR Discovery Framework?
questions.clinicalRationale: Problem, History, Experience, Expectation, Lifestyle, Frustration, Timeline, Barrier — eight pillars.

questions.question: A recommendation made before discovery is likely to be:
questions.clinicalRationale: Rushed recommendations feel generic and are easier for a patient to walk away from.

questions.question: "Barrier" in the discovery framework refers to:

questions.clinicalRationale: Barrier is the specific thing holding the patient back from a confident decision.

questions.question: Discovery questions should feel like:

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.title: Branch Manager SOP · Running the Branch — Revenue & Operations
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.reportsTo: Regional Head · Peer with Senior Doctor · Manages Reception, Counsellors, Therapists, Housekeeping
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.keyMotto: Run the branch as if it were yours. Hold the daily rhythm — the huddles, the doctor meeting, live verification, the debrief — and the branch holds its standard without heroics.

sections.title: 1 · Purpose & Scope
sections.content: This SOP defines how the Branch Manager runs the branch day to day. Revenue and operations are one job, held through a disciplined daily rhythm.

sections.title: 2 · Daily Operating Rhythm
sections.content:
Every day follows three distinct phases:
• Morning: Floor walk · reception, housekeeping & counsellor huddles · daily BM-Doctor meeting.
• Through the day: Verify consults · CRM audit · 2-hourly floor walks · asks register · doctor coordination.
• Evening: 6 PM counsellor debrief · compliance findings · daily log · WhatsApp summary to RH · plan tomorrow.

sections.title: 3 · Morning Procedure
sections.content:
1. Floor walk — reception, cabins, washrooms, refreshment area; look at the branch as a client would.
2. Reception huddle (5 min) — yesterday's score, today's appointments, VIPs, risks.
3. Housekeeping huddle (5 min) — same-day standards, asks from yesterday.
4. Counsellor huddle (10 min) — yesterday's follow-up list, today's expected consults, worried-about clients.
5. Daily meeting with the senior doctor.

sections.title: 4 · The Daily BM-Doctor Meeting — Peer Alignment
sections.content:
The single most important meeting of your day. Held every working day. Peers, not boss-and-subordinate. Minutes filed to corporate the same day.
Agenda — six items:
1. Target review — where the branch stands on revenue and clinical delivery this week.
2. Client challenges — specific clients with issues, complications, complaints.
3. Operational issues blocking clinical work.
4. Clinical issues affecting operations.
5. Growth-plan progress — what is working, what needs to change.
6. One ask each — one from the BM, one from the doctor.
MoM filing same day: Filed to Regional Head, Manisha, and Dr. Kanikta with owner and date.

sections.title: 5 · Through the Day & Evening Procedures
sections.content:
• Live-verify counsellor consultations — observe at least 2 per day.
• CRM audit — at least 5 of yesterday's records, looking for missing follow-ups, inflated promises, undocumented details.
• Floor walks every 2 hours — brief and visible to the team.
• Asks register — update the status of anything raised by any team member.
• 6 PM counsellor debrief (15 min) — standing questions in daily log.
• Daily WhatsApp summary to Regional Head — 5 lines: the numbers, one story, one worry, one ask.

sections.title: 6 · Hard-Line Rules — Never
sections.content:
• Never treat the senior doctor as a subordinate — the peer line is non-negotiable.
• Never skip the daily BM-Doctor meeting or file the MoM late.
• Never allow or direct a hard-line violation — off-system payments, outcome guarantees, fake conversions, floor-breach pricing.
• Never protect a failing team member out of personal loyalty, and never have favourites.
• Never hide a problem from the Regional Head.

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.title: Doctor (Branch) SOP · Clinical Delivery, Consultation & Coordination
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.reportsTo: Dr. Kanikta (Head of Clinical) · Peer with Branch Manager · Clinical lead for Therapists
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.keyMotto: Lead clinical. Consult every patient, document everything, set realistic expectations, convert ethically, and hold the peer line with the BM. Clinical safety and ethics come before any number.

sections.title: 1 · Consultation & Ethical Conversion — Per Patient
sections.content:
Consultation for every visit — no exceptions. Targets are ethical, not pushed: 90% overall, 65% to package. A patient counselled into a treatment they did not need is a clinical failure, not a sale.
1. Consult — diagnosis, assessment, and realistic expectations.
2. Record diagnosis, treatment plan, and product list in prescription/CRM.
3. Recommend the right plan; pitch clinically appropriate upsell/cross-sell ethically.
4. Align messaging with counsellor so the patient hears one unified story.
5. Add projection and next-visit plan.

sections.title: 2 · Clinical Supervision of Therapists
sections.content:
• Supervise delivery — spot-check cabins, timer discipline, protocol adherence.
• Sign off therapist competence; coach on specific gaps.
• Verify hygiene and sterilisation clinically.
• Track flagged / complex patients to resolution.

sections.title: 3 · Reaction & Safety Management
sections.content:
Clinical safety first, always. Manage reactions and complications immediately and correctly; never let an operational pressure override clinical judgement.
1. Manage any reaction or complication immediately, per protocol.
2. Record the event and the action taken.
3. Escalate any serious incident to Dr. Kanikta the same day.
4. Never guarantee an outcome; never treat off-protocol.

sections.title: 4 · Hard-Line Rules — Never
sections.content:
• Never let an operational decision override clinical judgement.
• Never treat the BM as a subordinate — or accept being managed by the BM.
• Never skip the daily BM-Doctor meeting or file the MoM late.
• Never guarantee an outcome or treat off-protocol under any pressure.
• Never compromise patient safety, consent or confidentiality.

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.title: Front Desk Manager (FDM) SOP · Daily Operations, Audit & Client Experience
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.reportsTo: Saurabh (Operations Manager) · Daily floor partner: Branch Manager · Coordinates with Senior Doctor
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.keyMotto: Hold the branch to operational standard, keep every client's experience clean and complaint-free, and prove it with audit evidence. Clinical judgement always stays with the doctor — the FDM owns operations, audit and experience.

sections.title: 1 · Hourly Floor Rounds & Cabin Audits
sections.content:
Every hour, a brief visible round checking waiting-area comfort, wait times, cabin readiness, hygiene, washroom standard, and staff conduct.
Therapist Cabin Audit (Operational):
Audit 1-2 cabins per day against:
1. Cabin prepared — clean linen replaced, surfaces wiped, instruments laid out, bin lined.
2. Session timer started and held — no rushed sessions, no overruns.
3. Verbal handoff done between cabins/therapists.
4. Cabin log completed for session.
5. Hygiene — hand sanitisation, single-use items, sterilisation evidence.
6. Machine clean and functional.

sections.title: 2 · Wait-Time & Complaint Recovery (L.E.A.R.N.)
sections.content:
Target: Clients attended within 5 minutes of arrival; average wait under 10 minutes.
Complaint Handling via L.E.A.R.N.:
• L — Listen: Let client finish without interrupting.
• E — Empathise: Acknowledge feeling; apologise for the experience.
• A — Act: Take ownership and state what you will do now.
• R — Resolve: Fix within your authority or escalate immediately.
• N — Note: Log in complaint register; close within 24h SLA. No DSAT carried forward without Saurabh knowing.

sections.title: 3 · Reception 10-Item Scorecard & Housekeeping Standard
sections.content:
1. Client greeted within 10 seconds, by name, with a smile.
2. Refreshment offered to every waiting client.
3. Warm, professional tone.
4. Front desk professional — no personal phone/screen, desk tidy.
5. Appointment located by name (never phone number).
6. Day schedule reviewed before opening.
7. Missed-call log maintained; calls returned same day.
8. Wait times communicated proactively.
9. Billing transparent — amount & purpose stated; WhatsApp receipt sent.
10. Client thanked on departure.

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.reportsTo: Front Desk Manager · Coordinates with Counsellor, Doctor, Housekeeping
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.keyMotto: A reception is not a desk. It is the first face a patient sees when she has spent weeks deciding to walk through that door, and the last voice she hears as she leaves carrying a story she will tell someone tonight.

sections.title: The Three Affirmations
sections.content:
1. The Welcome: 'Welcome to GLEUHR. Please come in.'
2. The Wait: 'Thank you so much for your patience. She'll be with you in just a few minutes.'
3. The Goodbye: 'Call us anytime, for anything. That's what we're here for.'

sections.title: The 10-Second Rule & Find-by-Name
sections.content: Greet in ten seconds; never ask for a phone number first. Look up immediately. Rise slightly or stand. Smile warmly. Appointments are always located by the client's name, never by asking 'give me your number'.

sections.title: The Phone Enquiry — First Contact Ever
sections.content: Pick up by third ring. Say: 'Good morning, GLEUHR Wellness, [your name] speaking. How can I help you today?' Resist quoting blind prices over the phone — invite for a diagnostic doctor consultation.

sections.title: The Post-Treatment Goodbye & Graceful Cancellation
sections.content: Walk her out, do not just nod. Say: 'Take care, [Name]ji. We'll see you on [date] at [time]... Call us anytime if you have questions about aftercare.' On cancellation, never make her feel chased: 'Of course, take your time. I'll leave your file open and you can message us whenever you're ready.'

sections.title: The Never List
sections.content:
• Never eat at the desk.
• Never have personal phone out.
• Never gossip in earshot.
• Never let a complaint be public in the waiting room.
• Never let a patient open a door you could have opened for her.
• Never skip the goodbye.

sections.content:

sections.title: Hourly Through-the-Day Checks

2. Bed, surfaces, and machine exterior wiped.
3. Waste bin cleared and relined (segregate clinical waste).
4. Cabin consumables restocked.
5. Signal cabin is ready to reception/therapist.

sections.title: Hard-Line Rules — Never
sections.content:
• Never skip washroom or cabin hygiene.
• Never mix clinical and general waste.
• Never reuse linen between patients.
• Never leave a client area unclean.
• Never ignore a spill or a hazard.

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.title: Branch Petty Cash, Expense Approval & Payment Process SOP

sections.content: Each Branch Manager is provided ₹4,000 for routine clinic expenses (tea/refreshments, drinking water, minor supplies). Petty cash must not be used to bypass the approval process.

sections.title: Expense Limit & Approval Matrix
sections.content:
• Below ₹500: BM petty cash. RH approval not required for routine expense. Airtable & Bill/Voucher mandatory.
• Exactly ₹500: Routine petty cash. Emergency ₹500 requires RH approval.
• Above ₹500: Payment through Finance/Deepa. RH approval MANDATORY before incurring expense.
• Emergency >₹500: Only with RH approval communicated to Deepa.

sections.title: ₹4,000 Replenishment Workflow
sections.content: Reconciliation-based replenishment system. When ₹4,000 is consumed, BM must submit complete utilization details (bills, date-wise expenses, Airtable entries) to RH. RH verifies and grants formal approval before Deepa releases the next ₹4,000.

sections.title: Prohibited Practices
sections.content:
• Splitting large expenses into smaller chunks to bypass the ₹500 rule.
• Using clinic funds for personal expenses.
• Claiming expenses without valid bills/vouchers.
• Requesting another ₹4,000 without reconciling the previous allocation.
• Delaying Airtable entries.

BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.title: Warehouse Operations, Stock Movement & Outbound Dispatch (SOP-OPS-001)
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.reportsTo: Purchase, Warehouse, Supply Chain & Finance Teams
BRANCH_STANDARDIZED_SOPS.keyMotto: Seamless stock movement, accurate SKU verification, and pre-approved external manpower allocation across hubs.

sections.title: Inbound Stock Movement Protocol
sections.content:
• Mandatory Notice: Purchase Team must inform Warehouse at least 24 hours prior to scheduled vehicle arrival.
• Emergency Shipments: Minimum 4 hours advance notice via official email + phone call.
• Mandatory Payload: ETA, vehicle type/size, driver contact, box/pallet count, SKU names, batch numbers, and PO/Challan reference.

sections.title: Manpower Planning & External Labour Protocol
sections.content: If regular staff is occupied with scheduled tasks, Warehouse Manager requests pre-approval for external labour from Operations/Supply Chain Head with box count and rate card. Verified payouts cleared by Finance within 2 business days.

sections.title: Outbound Dispatch Checklist
sections.content: Verify exact SKU names against Transfer Order, perform physical box count, inspect packaging integrity, and obtain driver's legible signature and phone number on Delivery Challan / LR.
